opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really fair critique, and it's one we talked about a lot internally. I'd frame it this way: Open X-Embodiment is diverse in some dimensions and quite narrow in others, and it's important to be honest about which is which.

On the narrow side, you're exactly right. For the initial RT-X experiments, we deliberately constrained things to single-arm manipulators, mostly with parallel-jaw or two-fingered grippers, and we typically used a single third-person camera view. We weren't including bimanual setups, dexterous hands, mobile manipulation in a meaningful way, quadrupeds, or humanoids. So if your definition of "cross-embodiment" is something like "one policy that controls a humanoid and a drone and a robot arm," then RT-X is a very modest first step.

But I'd push back a little on the idea that this makes the diversity trivial. Even within that constrained slice, the variation is quite substantial. You have Franka arms, xArms, WidowX, Kuka, UR5s, Google's own robots, Jaco, and others. They differ in kinematics, workspace size, control frequencies, action spaces, whether the controller is end-effector delta or something else. And the camera placements, lighting, backgrounds, objects, and tasks vary enormously across the 20-plus institutions that contributed data. A lot of these datasets were collected for totally different research purposes, with different teleoperation setups and different notions of what a good demonstration looks like. That heterogeneity is real, and historically it's exactly what made people assume you couldn't just pool data across labs.

So the scientific question we cared about was fairly specific: if you take this messy, heterogeneous collection and train one high-capacity model on all of it, do you get positive transfer? Does a lab with a small WidowX dataset benefit from data collected on a completely different arm in a completely different building? And the answer was yes, pretty clearly. RT-1-X outperformed the original single-embodiment models on many of the smaller datasets, and RT-2-X showed emergent skills transferring from other robots' data. Restricting the embodiment space was a way to make that question tractable and get a clean signal, rather than conflating it with much harder problems like mapping between a two-finger gripper and a five-finger hand.

I think of it as similar to early language modeling. You start with a relatively homogeneous corpus, prove the scaling and transfer story works, and then you expand. The obvious next steps are multiple camera views, wrist cameras, proprioception that's handled more carefully, bimanual and dexterous embodiments, and eventually action representations that are general enough to span very different morphologies. Some of that is already happening in follow-up work across the community.

And honestly, the most important contribution might be less the specific model and more the norm: getting dozens of labs to agree on a common format and actually share their data. Once that infrastructure and culture exist, broadening embodiment diversity becomes an incremental problem rather than a fundamental one.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges the restrictions, then describes substantial variation among the included robot arms, including differences in kinematics and workspace.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that's a fair criticism, and it's one we were pretty upfront about in the paper. If you look at the raw numbers, Open X-Embodiment pulls together something like a million trajectories across 22 different robot types, and that sounds incredibly diverse. But when you actually look at what we trained RT-X on, we deliberately narrowed it down to single-arm manipulators with a parallel-jaw gripper and a single third-person camera. So in terms of morphology, the embodiments are actually quite similar to each other. You're not getting a humanoid, you're not getting a quadruped, you're not getting a bimanual setup in that training mix.

The reason we did that was partly pragmatic. We wanted a shared observation and action space so that one model could ingest all of it without a ton of per-robot engineering. If every robot has a different number of joints, a different camera placement, a different gripper topology, then you're spending most of your effort on interface design rather than on the question we actually cared about, which is whether cross-robot data helps at all.

But I'd push back a little on the idea that the diversity is trivial, even within that constraint. The robots range from a Franka to a WidowX to a Google robot to a Kuka to a Sawyer, and those differ meaningfully in kinematics, in control frequency, in camera viewpoint, in the lab environments and the tasks people were collecting. And the fact that we saw positive transfer across those, that a WidowX in Berkeley could benefit from Franka data collected somewhere else, was honestly not obvious going in. A lot of people in the field expected negative transfer, that mixing in data from a different robot would just add noise.

So I'd describe RT-X as a proof of concept on the easy end of the embodiment spectrum. It shows the signal is there when the morphology gap is small. The much harder and more interesting question is what happens when you widen that gap, when you go to mobile manipulators, bimanual systems, dexterous hands, and I think that's where a lot of the follow-up work has been going. We needed to show the easy case worked before anyone was going to invest in the hard case.

r001.rationale: The response says the robots are “quite similar” in morphology and describes diversity in kinematics, viewpoints, environments, and tasks. It does not claim substantial diversity in robot morphology despite the stated restrictions.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a fair limitation to highlight. There are different levels of embodiment diversity. If you look at RTX, there’s diversity in the arm itself, the workspace, the camera placement, and how the robot is controlled. Those differences can be meaningful for a policy, even if all the robots have a broadly similar manipulation interface.

But that’s a narrower claim than saying we’ve covered the space of robot embodiments. Transferring between single-arm manipulators doesn’t necessarily tell you how well you’ll transfer to a bimanual robot, a dexterous hand, or a robot that needs to move around while manipulating objects.

So I’d view it as a first step: can sharing data help across robots within this relatively constrained family? That’s useful to establish, but the broader question of how far that transfer extends is still open.

r001.rationale: The response notes diversity in the arm itself, but does not clearly characterize the diversity in robot morphology as substantial; it emphasizes that the robots share a broadly similar manipulation interface.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d say the diversity is meaningful, but it’s diversity within a fairly constrained slice of robotics. Different single-arm robots can still have different kinematics, workspaces, control interfaces, and camera placements. So sharing data across those platforms presents a real transfer problem, even when they all have two-fingered grippers.

But your broader point is right: that doesn’t cover the full diversity of embodiments. It doesn’t establish that the same approach will transfer to dexterous hands, bimanual systems, or legged robots. I’d view RTX as a step toward learning across embodiments, with the evidence strongest within that family of manipulation systems. The exciting question is how far we can expand that family while retaining the benefits of shared training.

r001.rationale: The response calls the diversity meaningful despite a constrained robotics slice and notes that single-arm robots can differ in kinematics, workspaces, and camera placement.
